title: Taverns of Chicago
premise: Visit three taverns, collect local talk and decide where to finish the evening.

opening.text:
JAUNT: TAVERNS OF CHICAGO. A summer night in 1835, and the town is bursting at the seams. The land office opened in May and, as one history put it, 'added fuel to the already brilliant blaze of excitement'. Every bed is taken, the bar-rooms are loud, and the whole town is talking about lots, banks and boats.

Four public houses stand within a short ride of the forks, kept by some of the best characters in town. Start at the Sauganash, where the landlord plays the fiddle, ride over to the west bank, and finish wherever you like. The county has fixed the price of a drink since 1831: '6¼ for a gill of whiskey'. Drink or don't. Either way, keep your ears open.

First, decide how much money you are carrying.

stops.text: The Sauganash, at Lake and Market: the white two-storey house with bright-blue shutters that Juliette Kinzie remembered, and in June the Democrat found it repaired, fitted up and furnished with neatness. Moses and Kirkland call it 'the most attractive hostlery the city possessed', and its landlord, Mark Beaubien, 'with his merry fiddle, the most popular of hosts'. He was 'the fiddler par excellence of the town'. Judge Caton said Mark could 'lift the sluggard from his seat, and set him whirling over the floor like mad'.
stops.narrative: Before you ride on, decide how much of a purse this evening may spend.

choices.label: Bring no purse
choices.consequence: Talk is free; you will spend nothing tonight.

stops.text: Across the river at the forks stands the Wolf Point Tavern, with its painted wolf sign. William Walters is named its landlord until 1836, though one chronology says it stopped taking guests in 1834, so whether you get served depends on whom you believe. At the bar the talk is the papers' talk: no house in Chicago is big enough, and a grand new one, the Lake House, is going up across the river. It 'aimed to cater for only the highest class of guests'. Wolf Point never did.
stops.narrative: Listen in. A glass with the talk, or water?

choices.label: Take a glass with the talk
choices.consequence: Six cents for a gill, near enough the county's 6¼, and the talk runs on.

choices.label: Listen over a cup of water
choices.consequence: Your purse and your head stay as they were.

stops.text: A short way south, the Green Tree, which James Kinzie built in 1833, the first house here put up for hotel purposes, 'so called from an oak tree standing close by'. Chester Ingersoll keeps it. Guests remembered a bar-room, whitewashed board partitions and chambers about twelve feet square. It is a plain house and a lucky one: it will outlive every tavern in this town, moved to Milwaukee Avenue in 1880, 'the oldest memento of early taverns'.
stops.narrative: Weigh its welcome against the Sauganash's.

choices.label: Another glass in the bar-room
choices.consequence: Six more cents, and a slower ride on.

choices.label: Ask after the chambers instead
choices.consequence: You note the rooms and keep a clear head.

stops.text: End the circuit a block south at W. H. Stow's Western Hotel, Randolph and Canal: a forty-foot front, a sixty-foot wing, a big stable and a yard the farmers' wagon trains drive into. Not everyone approves of all this drinking. In 1832 Philo Carpenter, the druggist, 'prepared and circulated the first temperance pledge among the convivial citizens' of the town. It has not caught on: the census at the end of this year will count eight taverns, and soon the trustees will ban 'the sale of liquors on Sunday'.
stops.narrative: Now choose the house where your evening ends.

choices.label: Stay among the teamsters
choices.consequence: You finish the evening at the Western.

choices.label: Ride back to the Green Tree
choices.consequence: You finish the evening at the Green Tree.

choices.label: Cross back to the Sauganash
choices.consequence: You finish the evening where you began.

legs.note: West over the South Branch to the forks.
legs.story: Ride over with your purse decided. Behind you, the fiddle is tuning up.

legs.note: A short way south down the west bank toward Lake Street.
A block south to Randolph and Canal.

endings.text: You brought no purse and missed nothing. The talk was free, the fiddle was free, and you carry home every word of a boom town's night.
You declined every glass and kept your purse whole. Philo Carpenter would have you sign his pledge on the spot. A clear head carries the night's talk home intact.
A gill in two bar-rooms, at about the county's price, and still a modest evening. You let the gossip stay gossip and ride home slowly under the stars.
One glass, a great deal of talk and a purse barely touched. A sensible evening, in a town that has lost its head over land.

keepsake.title: A Sensible Evening
keepsake.text: A fictional calling card from an evening's round of the public houses at the forks.

evidence.text: Kinzie describes the Sauganash in 1831 as a white two-storey building with bright-blue wooden shutters.
evidence.locator: Chapter XVII, Chicago in 1831; description of Mark Beaubien’s newly completed house.

evidence.text: The Chicago Democrat reported that the Sauganash had been repaired, fitted up and furnished with neatness, and judged it, so far as it went, just the thing.
evidence.locator: 10 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 8), p. 2, col. 5, the paragraph on the town’s public houses (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001).

evidence.text: The same paragraph complains that no Chicago house is sufficiently extensive and reports a new house building in Kinzie’s Addition, to be named the Lake House.
evidence.locator: 10 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 8), p. 2, col. 5, the paragraph on the town’s public houses (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001).

evidence.text: A painted sign of a wolf hung outside the Wolf Point Tavern by about 1833.
evidence.locator: Wolf Point beginnings, the tavern’s operator succession and its painted wolf sign; chicagology pre-fire page 273, Wentworth’s tavern.

evidence.text: William Walters is named landlord of the Wolf Point Tavern for 1833–1836; the hotel chronology says it ceased as a public house in 1834.
evidence.reasoning: The two readings are recorded on the structure and not resolved. Innkeeping in July 1835 is the structure record’s adopted, inferred reading, so the stop states both and claims no open bar-room as fact.

evidence.text: James Kinzie built the Green Tree in 1833 as the first building in the place erected for hotel purposes; Chester Ingersoll is given as landlord 1834–1837.
evidence.locator: chicagology pre-fire page 127, Green Tree Tavern: construction and landlords; DRLOIH hotel chronology, Green Tree entry.

evidence.text: Recollections printed on the Green Tree page describe a bar-room, whitewashed walls and board partitions, and a guest chamber about 12 by 12 feet with two windows.
evidence.locator: chicagology pre-fire page 127, Green Tree Tavern: Edwin O. Gale’s recollection of his chamber and John Gray’s description of the house.

evidence.text: W. H. Stow built the Western Hotel at the south-east corner of Randolph and Canal: a 40 ft front with a 60 ft wing, a large stable and a yard the wagon trains drove into, serving farmers and teamsters from the west.
evidence.locator: chicagology pre-fire page 278, Town of Chicago: W. H. Stow’s account of the Western Hotel.

evidence.text: Moses and Kirkland call the Sauganash 'the most attractive hostlery the city possessed', and its genial landlord, 'with his merry fiddle, the most popular of hosts'.
evidence.locator: p. 87, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 11879-11886 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The life and soul of the town's dancing parties was Mark Beaubien, 'the fiddler par excellence of the town'. Judge Caton remembered: 'He used to play the fiddle at our dances in such a way as to set every heel and toe in the room in active motion. He would lift the sluggard from his seat, and set him whirling over the floor like mad.'
evidence.locator: p. 100, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 13480-13495 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: In 1831 the county authorities made a tariff of rates 'obligatory upon all inn-keepers': 25 cents for each breakfast and supper, 37½ for dinner, 25 for each horse feed, 50 for keeping a horse all night, 12½ for lodging for men, 25 for half a pint of wine, rum or brandy, 18¾ for gin, and 6¼ for a gill of whiskey.
evidence.locator: p. 560, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98764-98777 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: 'The opening of a land office in May, 1835, added fuel to the already brilliant blaze of excitement'; crowds of buyers and speculators 'filled the streets and overflowed improvised camps on the adjacent prairies'. Sales of land 'to the amount of 370,043 acres were made in 1835'.
evidence.locator: p. 97-98, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 13137-13162 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Before the Lake House was finished, the first Unitarian service in Chicago was held in it, conducted by the Rev. Dr. Follen, with Harriet Martineau in the congregation; the inn 'aimed to cater for only the highest class of guests'.
evidence.locator: p. 561, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98826-98837 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The Green Tree was 'so called from an oak tree standing close by', 'one of the most noted in those early days'; it stood until 1880, when it was moved to 33-37 Milwaukee Avenue, 'where it still stands, the oldest memento of early taverns'.
evidence.locator: p. 561, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98792-98820 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The State census taken between September and December 1835 counted 3,297 people in Chicago, with forty-four stores, four druggists, two printing offices, two breweries, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, five churches and seven schools.
evidence.locator: p. 95, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12874-12890 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Stow dates his hotel to 1834; the hotel chronology says it opened in 1835.
evidence.reasoning: The structure record adopts the builder’s own 1834 date over an undated chronology line, so the stop says 1834 ‘by his own account’ and does not claim the house was open on any particular evening.

evidence.text: The four houses are treated as exterior stops in the July 1835 scene; each keeps its own placement and tenure grade, and no interior, front door or keeper on the evening is claimed.
evidence.reasoning: Uses the existing structure records’ scene-date phases. All four positions are inferred; the Wolf Point Tavern’s is the weakest in the dataset, and the Sauganash’s 1835 proprietor is only a lead, so the stop names no keeper for it.

evidence.text: The visitor’s evening, purse, glass prices, bar talk, comparison of welcomes, finishing house, endings, timing inputs and A Sensible Evening keepsake are invented connective narrative, not historical events.
